subject: Biology
title: Reef Biodiversity
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Reef Biodiversity.

hook.text: Coral reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but support 25% of all marine species.

buildup.text: The complex 3D structure of reefs creates countless hiding spots, nurseries, and hunting grounds.

discovery.text: Parrotfish eat coral and excrete sand. One parrotfish produces up to 300 kg of sand per year.

twist.text: Many reef fish change sex during their lives. Clownfish are born male and the dominant one becomes female.

climax.text: Reefs are called the 'rainforests of the sea'—and they're disappearing even faster.

punchline.text: 1% of the floor. 25% of the life. Every species matters.

quiz.question: What do parrotfish produce by eating coral?

details.summary: Coral reefs occupy less than 0.1 percent of the ocean floor but support roughly 25 percent of all marine species. This extraordinary biodiversity rivals tropical rainforests and results from the complex three-dimensional structure reefs provide across countless microhabitats.
details.whyItMatters: Reef biodiversity underpins fisheries feeding hundreds of millions of people and contains untapped sources of medicines and biological compounds. Losing reefs means losing an irreplaceable reservoir of marine life and genetic diversity.
takeaways: Reefs support approximately 25 percent of all marine species in 0.1 percent of ocean area
The structural complexity of reefs creates thousands of microhabitats for species
Many reef species are still undiscovered with estimates of 1 to 9 million total

faq.question: Why are coral reefs so much more diverse than surrounding ocean?
faq.answer: Reef structure creates an enormous variety of microhabitats: crevices, caves, overhangs, sandy patches, and rubble zones. Stable tropical temperatures, clear water, and the three-dimensional complexity support specialized niches for thousands of species in a small area.

faq.question: How many species live on coral reefs?
faq.answer: Known reef species number around 60,000, but estimates of total reef biodiversity range from 1 to 9 million species. Many are tiny invertebrates, cryptic fish, or microorganisms hidden within the reef structure that have never been formally described.
